notes.b: Melting and boiling are about the attractions between molecules, not the bonds inside them. Intermolecular forces (the attractions between separate molecules) decide how much energy a molecular substance needs to change state.
points: To melt or boil a molecular substance (one made of separate small molecules), energy must be supplied to overcome the intermolecular forces, so the molecules can move apart.
The stronger the intermolecular forces, the higher the melting and boiling points, because more energy is needed to pull the molecules apart.

Substances with only London dispersion forces (weak attractions caused by temporary uneven electron distribution) between small molecules are gases at room temperature, because the forces are too weak to hold them together. Methane is an example: it boils at −162 °C.
Group 14 hydrides (compounds of hydrogen with the group 14 elements) rise steadily in boiling point: CH₄ < SiH₄ < GeH₄ < SnH₄.

Hydrogen bonding (a strong intermolecular attraction involving hydrogen) gives unusually high boiling points. Water boils at 100 °C, but hydrogen sulfide, a heavier molecule with no hydrogen bonding, boils at −60 °C.
notes.tip: Boiling breaks intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds. Say this whenever you explain a boiling point. To explain why water boils far higher than hydrogen sulfide, point to hydrogen bonding, even though hydrogen sulfide molecules have the greater mass.

notes.b: Whether one substance dissolves in another depends on the attractions between their particles. The solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving and the solute is the substance that dissolves.
points: A substance dissolves when the attractions between solvent and solute particles are similar to or stronger than the attractions they replace. This is summed up as “like dissolves like”.

Polar substances (those whose molecules have a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end) and hydrogen-bonding substances such as ethanol, ammonia and sugar dissolve in water, because they form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
Non-polar substances such as iodine, hexane and oils do not dissolve in water. They dissolve in non-polar solvents such as cyclohexane, where the London forces are similar to those they replace.
Hexane and water do not mix, which means they form two layers.
notes.tip: To explain why ethanol dissolves in water but hexane does not, say that ethanol forms hydrogen bonds with water, while hexane is non-polar and has only London forces, which are not similar to the attractions in water.

notes.b: Water is a very small molecule, yet it behaves unlike other small molecules. The reason is hydrogen bonding between its molecules.
points: Water has a high boiling point and a high melting point for such a small molecule, because the hydrogen bonds between molecules take a lot of energy to overcome.
Ice is less dense than liquid water: hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice (a regular arrangement with gaps between molecules), so ice floats.
Water is a good solvent for ionic and polar substances, because it can form attractions with them.

notes.b: Secondary data means results taken from tables or graphs rather than measured yourself. The boiling points below (bp) are the sample data you may be asked to interpret.
points: Noble gas boiling points (the noble gases are the group 18 elements): He −269 °C; Ne −246 °C; Ar −186 °C; Kr −153 °C; Xe −108 °C.
Halogens (the group 17 elements) at room temperature: fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid.
Alkane (hydrocarbon) boiling points: methane −162 °C; ethane −89 °C; propane −42 °C; butane −1 °C; pentane 36 °C; hexane 69 °C.
Group 16 hydride boiling points: H₂O 100 °C; H₂S −60 °C; H₂Se −41 °C; H₂Te −2 °C.
Group 15 and 17 hydride boiling points: NH₃ −33 °C vs PH₃ −88 °C; HF 20 °C vs HCl −85 °C.
Compounds of similar mass: ethanol (bp 78 °C, hydrogen bonding) vs propane (bp −42 °C, London forces only).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain the trend in boiling points of the halogens, noble gases or alkanes, and why ethanol and water behave differently. Quote values from the data and link each to the type of intermolecular force. At Ordinary Level you relate each property to the force type.

notes.b: At Higher Level you must explain why the boiling points in the data follow their patterns. Two ideas do all the work: London forces grow with molecule size, and hydrogen bonding lifts a boiling point far above the trend.
points: Down group 18, down group 17 and along the alkane series, boiling points rise because the molecules have more electrons and larger electron clouds, so London dispersion forces get stronger.
In the group 16 hydrides, boiling point rises from H₂S to H₂Te as London forces increase with size. Water is far higher than the trend predicts because of hydrogen bonding.
The same anomaly (a value far out of line with the trend) appears for NH₃ in group 15 and HF in group 17, which both form hydrogen bonds.

Molecules of similar mass have higher boiling points if they are polar (attracted by dipole–dipole forces, the attractions between opposite ends of polar molecules), and much higher ones if they hydrogen bond, e.g. ethanol compared with propane.
Diagram: a graph of boiling point against period for the hydrides of groups 14, 15, 16 and 17, showing the high values of H₂O, HF and NH₃ and the steady rise from CH₄ to SnH₄.
notes.tip: Accounting for a trend means giving the reason, not just describing it. For the halogens, noble gases and alkanes the reason is stronger London forces from more electrons. For water the reason is hydrogen bonding.

notes.h: Polar bonds and polar molecules (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Some bonds share electrons unequally, but that does not always make the whole molecule polar. Whether it does depends on the shape, which is stated here rather than worked out.
points: A polar bond has an uneven share of electrons, giving a slightly positive end (δ+) and a slightly negative end (δ−).
A polar molecule has an overall uneven distribution of charge, with a δ+ end and a δ− end.
Whether a molecule is polar depends on both its bonds and its shape: polar bonds arranged symmetrically cancel out, so the molecule has no δ+ or δ− end.
notes.tip: Polar bonds do not always make a polar molecule. Always check the shape before you decide.

notes.h: Symmetry and cancelling dipoles (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A dipole is the pair of δ+ and δ− ends of a polar bond. In a symmetrical molecule the dipoles pull in opposite directions and cancel, while in an unsymmetrical molecule they add up.
points: Carbon dioxide: each C=O bond is polar, but the molecule is linear (O=C=O, in a straight line), so the two bond polarities point in opposite directions and cancel; CO₂ is non-polar.
Tetrachloromethane (CCl₄): four polar C–Cl bonds arranged tetrahedrally (pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron) cancel; CCl₄ is non-polar.
Boron trifluoride (BF₃): three polar B–F bonds at 120° in a trigonal plane (flat, evenly spaced) cancel; BF₃ is non-polar.
Water: two polar O–H bonds in a V-shaped (bent) molecule do not cancel, so water is polar, with δ− on oxygen.
Ammonia: three polar N–H bonds in a pyramidal molecule (a shape like a pyramid, with nitrogen at the top) do not cancel, so NH₃ is polar.
Trichloromethane (CHCl₃): the C–H bond differs from the three C–Cl bonds, so the tetrahedral molecule is unsymmetrical and polar.
Diagram: CO₂, CCl₄, H₂O and NH₃, with arrows (or δ+ and δ− labels) on each bond showing whether the polarities cancel; label each molecule polar or non-polar.
notes.tip: Exams ask why carbon dioxide is non-polar although its bonds are polar, and why water is polar but tetrachloromethane is not. Name the shape, say the bond polarities cancel or do not, and give the result. Do not quote dipole moment values or units.

notes.h: Effect on intermolecular forces (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Polarity decides which intermolecular forces act between molecules. Those forces then set the boiling point and the solubility.
points: Polar molecules attract each other by permanent dipole–dipole forces (or hydrogen bonds) as well as London dispersion forces, so they have stronger intermolecular forces than non-polar molecules of similar size.

Non-polar molecules, including symmetrical ones with polar bonds, have only London dispersion forces between them. For example, carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature, and tetrachloromethane is immiscible with water (does not mix with it).
A symmetrical molecule usually has a lower boiling point and lower solubility in water than an unsymmetrical one of similar size, because its forces between molecules are weaker.
Tetrachloromethane is immiscible with water, while trichloromethane is slightly soluble; both dissolve in non-polar solvents.
notes.tip: When asked about the intermolecular forces in carbon dioxide and in water, say which forces each has. Water is polar, with dipole–dipole forces or hydrogen bonds plus London forces. Carbon dioxide is non-polar, with only London forces.

notes.b: A molecule can contain polar bonds and still be non-polar overall. What matters is the shape. These shapes are stated, not derived.
points: A molecule with polar bonds is polar overall only if its shape is unsymmetrical, so that its charge is unevenly spread.
Water is V-shaped (bent), so it is polar.
Ammonia is pyramidal, so it is polar.
Carbon dioxide is linear and methane is tetrahedral: both are non-polar.
notes.tip: State the shape rather than working it out. Predicting the polarity of a molecule from its shape is a topic exams ask.

notes.b: Once you know a molecule's shape and polarity, you can predict its boiling point and what it dissolves in.
points: Polar molecules have stronger forces between them than non-polar molecules of similar size, so they have higher boiling points.
Polar molecules tend to dissolve in polar solvents such as water; non-polar molecules dissolve in non-polar solvents such as cyclohexane.
Water is a liquid at room temperature and dissolves salts, because it is polar and forms hydrogen bonds; methane is a non-polar gas and is almost insoluble in water.
Ammonia, which is polar, is very soluble in water; carbon dioxide, which is non-polar, is only slightly soluble.
notes.tip: To explain why water is a liquid and methane a gas, use the shape and polarity of each molecule: water is polar and bent, methane is non-polar and tetrahedral, so water has the stronger forces between molecules.

notes.h: Investigation: testing liquids for polarity with a charged rod (set-up)
notes.b: Polar molecules respond to an electric charge and non-polar ones do not. A charged rod held beside a thin stream of liquid shows which kind a liquid is made of.
points: Aim: to show whether a liquid is made of polar molecules.
Apparatus: a burette (a long graduated tube with a tap) clamped above a beaker, a polythene (or acetate) rod, a cloth, and liquids such as water and cyclohexane.
Diagram: a burette clamped above a beaker, releasing a thin stream of liquid; label the burette, the beaker and the stream.
Diagram: a charged polythene rod held beside the stream, with the stream bending towards it; label the rod, the stream and the direction of deflection (the sideways bend).
Independent variable (the one you change): the liquid tested.
Dependent variable (the one you observe): whether the stream is deflected.
Controlled variables (kept the same): the same rod and cloth, with the rod recharged before each test, so that every liquid meets a charged rod.

notes.b: The method is the same for each liquid, and comparing the two streams gives the conclusion.
points: Step 1: Charge the rod by rubbing it with the cloth.
Step 2: Let a thin stream of the liquid run from the burette, and hold the rod close to the stream without touching it.
Step 3: Repeat with the other liquid, recharging the rod each time.
Result: the stream of water is deflected (attracted) towards the rod; the stream of cyclohexane is not deflected.
The water stream is attracted to the rod whether the rod is charged positively or negatively, because the molecules rotate.
Explanation: polar molecules turn so that their oppositely charged end faces the rod and are attracted to it; non-polar molecules are not attracted.
Safety: cyclohexane is flammable and harmful, so use no flames, small volumes and good ventilation, and collect it for disposal.
notes.tip: A question may ask you to describe how to show that water is polar using a charged rod. Give the apparatus, the three steps, the result for each liquid and the explanation. Remember the water is attracted whether the rod is positive or negative.

keyTerms.definition: The temperature at which a liquid's vapour pressure equals the atmospheric pressure and it boils.
The extent to which a solute dissolves in a solvent at a stated temperature.
The principle that substances dissolve readily in solvents with similar types of intermolecular forces.
The liquid in which a solute dissolves to form a solution.
The substance that dissolves in a solvent.
A substance whose molecules contain H bonded to F, O or N, so that they form hydrogen bonds.
The spaced-out arrangement of molecules in ice, held by hydrogen bonds, that makes ice less dense than liquid water.
Describes two liquids that do not mix and form separate layers, such as hexane and water.
A covalent bond in which the shared electrons are drawn unevenly, giving δ+ and δ− ends.
A molecule with an overall uneven distribution of charge, so that it has a δ+ end and a δ− end.
A molecule whose charge is evenly distributed overall, either because it has no polar bonds or because its polar bonds cancel.
Polar bonds whose polarities point in opposite or balancing directions, so that they give no overall polarity.
A molecule whose shape is arranged so that its bond polarities balance, such as a linear or tetrahedral molecule with identical bonds.
A flat shape in which three bonded atoms lie at 120° to one another around a central atom.
A solvent made of polar molecules, such as water, that dissolves ionic and polar substances.
A solvent made of non-polar molecules, such as cyclohexane, that dissolves non-polar substances.
A molecule with two bonded atoms at an angle to a central atom, such as water.
A molecule with three bonded atoms arranged in a pyramid above a central atom, such as ammonia.
A molecule with four bonded atoms arranged at the corners of a tetrahedron around a central atom, such as methane.
A molecule whose atoms lie in a straight line, such as carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Explain why water has a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulfide, even though hydrogen sulfide molecules have a greater mass.
questions.model: Both are molecular compounds, so boiling overcomes the intermolecular forces between molecules, not the covalent bonds within them. Water molecules form hydrogen bonds, which are the strongest intermolecular forces here, so a lot of energy is needed to overcome them; water boils at 100 °C. Hydrogen sulfide molecules are heavier, so their London dispersion forces are larger than those of a lighter molecule, but they have no hydrogen bonding and the forces between them are weaker overall. Hydrogen sulfide boils at −60 °C.

questions.prompt: Account for the trend in boiling points down group 17 from fluorine to iodine.
questions.model: Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid at room temperature. Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are all non-polar molecules, so the only intermolecular forces are London dispersion forces. Down group 17 the molecules have more electrons and larger electron clouds, so the London dispersion forces get stronger. More energy is needed to overcome the stronger forces, so the boiling points rise down the group.

questions.prompt: Explain why ethanol is soluble in water but hexane is not.
questions.model: Ethanol is polar and forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules. The attractions between ethanol and water are similar to or stronger than the hydrogen bonds between water molecules that they replace, so ethanol dissolves: like dissolves like. Hexane is non-polar and has only London dispersion forces. These are too weak to replace the hydrogen bonds between water molecules, so hexane does not dissolve and forms two layers with water.

questions.prompt: Explain why the carbon dioxide molecule is non-polar but the water molecule is polar, although both contain polar bonds, and state the effect of this on the intermolecular forces in each.
questions.model: Carbon dioxide has polar C=O bonds, but its molecule is linear, so the two bond polarities point in opposite directions and cancel; the molecule is non-polar. Water has two polar O–H bonds in a V-shaped molecule, so they do not cancel; water is polar, with δ− on oxygen. Polar water molecules have permanent dipole–dipole forces (and hydrogen bonds) as well as London dispersion forces between them, so their intermolecular forces are stronger. Non-polar carbon dioxide molecules have only London dispersion forces between them, so their intermolecular forces are weaker.

questions.prompt: Tetrachloromethane (CCl₄) is non-polar but trichloromethane (CHCl₃) is polar. Explain.
questions.model: Tetrachloromethane has four polar C–Cl bonds arranged tetrahedrally, so they cancel and the molecule is non-polar. Trichloromethane has a C–H bond that differs from its three C–Cl bonds, so the tetrahedral molecule is unsymmetrical; its polarities do not cancel and the molecule is polar.

questions.prompt: Describe an experiment to show that water molecules are polar and cyclohexane molecules are not, and explain the results.
questions.model: Charge a polythene rod by rubbing it with a cloth. Let a thin stream of water run from a burette and hold the charged rod close to the stream without touching it; the water stream is deflected towards the rod. Repeat with cyclohexane, recharging the rod each time; the stream is not deflected. Explanation: water molecules are polar, with a δ+ end and a δ− end. They turn so that their oppositely charged end faces the rod and are attracted to it. Cyclohexane molecules are non-polar, so they are not attracted to the rod. Safety: cyclohexane is flammable and harmful, so use no flames, small volumes and good ventilation.

questions.prompt: Methane and water have similar relative molecular masses. Use the shape and polarity of each molecule to explain why water is a liquid at room temperature and methane is a gas.
questions.model: Water is a V-shaped molecule with polar O–H bonds that do not cancel, so it is polar. Its polar molecules have stronger forces between them, including hydrogen bonds, so more energy is needed to overcome them and water is a liquid at room temperature. Methane is a tetrahedral, non-polar molecule, so its molecules have only weak London dispersion forces between them, and it is a gas at room temperature.
